purpose: Amoxapine is used to treat depression, including depression that comes with anxiety or agitation. It helps improve your mood, energy level, and overall sense of well-being. Your doctor may also use it to treat other conditions as they see fit.
how_it_works: Amoxapine works by boosting the levels of certain natural chemicals in your brain, mainly serotonin and norepinephrine, which help regulate mood. Think of these chemicals as messengers that help brain cells communicate — when they are balanced, you tend to feel better emotionally. It also has some unique properties similar to antipsychotic medications, which can help with more severe depression.
common_side_effects: Drowsiness or feeling sleepy, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, dizziness when standing up too fast, weight gain, increased sweating, and headache. Most of these tend to improve after your body adjusts to the medication.
warnings: Do not stop taking this medication suddenly without talking to your doctor, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms. It carries a black box warning for increased risk of suicidal thoughts, especially in people under 25, so contact your doctor right away if you notice worsening mood or new thoughts of self-harm. Avoid alcohol while taking this drug. Rare but serious side effects include a movement disorder called tardive dyskinesia and a dangerous condition called neuroleptic malignant syndrome — seek emergency help if you develop muscle stiffness, high fever, or confusion. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, especially MAOIs, as combining them can be life-threatening.
typical_dosing: Adults usually start with 50 mg taken 2 to 3 times a day. Your doctor may gradually increase your dose, typically up to 150 to 300 mg per day depending on how you respond. Some patients may take their full daily dose at bedtime to reduce daytime drowsiness. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribes.
